title: Conservation laws, extended polymatroids and multiarmed bandit problems; a polyhedral approach to indexable systems
contribution: Shows that performance vectors satisfying generalized conservation laws span an extended polymatroid whose vertices are static-priority policies, so that LP duality and a one-pass adaptive greedy algorithm give optimal priority-index policies, Gittins indices as sums of dual variables, a sufficient decomposition condition and closed formulas for branching bandits, Klimov's queue and multiarmed bandits.
problem_entry: SD+LO: stochastic scheduling relies on dynamic programming and 'ingenious but often ad hoc methods', while mathematical programming describes feasible spaces (p. 1); a survey's complaint about scattered results (pp. 1-2) and a 14-row table of indexable problems (p. 3) lead to the question why these problems have efficient solutions, and whether a general polyhedral approach explains indexability and decomposability (pp. 3-4). A stated-joint SD method: describe the feasible space as a polyhedron and attack it with mathematical programming (p. 3).
key_idea: Generalized conservation laws with weights A_i^S (Definition 5, pp. 19-20) make the achievable region an extended polymatroid whose vertices are the priority policies (Theorem 4, p. 20); adaptive greedy solves the LP (Proposition 1, pp. 11-12), and the summed dual variables are the (Gittins) indices (Definition 4, p. 13; p. 41); one model, branching bandits, covers the classical cases (pp. 22-23).
assumptions: Branching bandits: a single server, finite classes, random service and offspring with an arbitrary joint law; nonanticipative, nonidling, nonpreemptive policies (p. 23). Criteria: discounted reward-tax (p. 24), or undiscounted tax with the spectral radius of E[N] below 1 and finite expectations, the promised necessary and sufficient conditions never given (pp. 32-33). Assumption 1 defines the polytope class (p. 9); Assumption 2 is needed for decomposition (p. 17); the fixed point has no closed form in general (p. 32); no data.
proof_devices: LP-duality proof of adaptive greedy: a dual solution on a nested family, dual feasibility by induction, complementary slackness (Proposition 1, pp. 11-12)

Vertices = priority vectors, since each vertex uniquely maximizes a linear objective and the algorithm returns some v(pi) (Theorem 1, p. 13); with A = 1 it is Edmonds' greedy, so b is submodular (p. 13)
Tie-free algorithm returning a partition makes the indices well defined; equivalent optimality conditions give an O(n log n) test and a closed-form optimal value (Propositions 2-3, pp. 14-16)
Index decomposition under Assumption 2 (Theorem 3, pp. 17-18), failing in general for Klimov's problem (p. 18)
Conservation laws: busy-period partition for the equality (Proposition 4, pp. 23-24) and a sample-path interchange for the inequality (Figure 5, pp. 28-29, 35-36)
Bell's entrance-charge and departure-refund accounting turns taxes into rewards (p. 25); a retirement option shows index = break-even pension (Proposition 5, p. 30)
Parameters from Laplace-transform fixed points (Proposition 6, pp. 31-32), or from linear systems in the undiscounted case (pp. 37-38)

Optimal bandit reward as E[max of independent random indices] via a product form of b, giving submodularity (Theorem 12, Corollary 5, pp. 43-44); equivalence with the Varaiya-Walrand-Buyukkoc algorithm by induction (Proposition 9, p. 42)
Arrival-rate invariance of Klimov's priorities by algebraic rescaling (pp. 46-47)
experiments: none: pure theory; operation counts (p. 12) and the same complexity as the fastest known off-line Gittins-index algorithm (p. 42).
positioning: Generalizes Shanthikumar-Yao (all weights 1 give polymatroids, p. 20) and builds on Tsoucas's extended polymatroids and his direct proof (pp. 9-10, 12); explicit credit to Weber, Whittle, Lai-Ying and Nain-Tsoucas-Walrand (pp. 30, 44, 47); one specific critique: Tsoucas gives no closed forms and a bottom-up algorithm (p. 46); Glazebrook had already used the polyhedral results (p. 16).
writing: Ten consequences in the abstract and eleven in the introduction (pp. 1, 4); a worked two-armed bandit before the theory (pp. 5-8); three mapping tables (pp. 3, 19, 38); low hedging, a two-sentence conclusion (p. 48); the abstract's 'characterization' of indexable systems is proved only in the sufficient direction (pp. 1, 4, 20-21).
limits_future: Limits in the body: Klimov's indices are not decomposable in general (p. 18); no closed-form fixed point (p. 32); finite expectations assumed (p. 33); nonlinear objectives delegated (p. 22); single-server scope, with networks only via a companion bounds paper (p. 4). No future work is stated (p. 48).

method_links.note: Template for steps 1-4: it names the owning DP tradition, takes performance vectors as variables, keeps the region an LP feasible set through conservation laws, and reads the indices off the dual as sums of dual variables ('a purely algebraic characterization') and as break-even pensions. The boundary is only partly printed. SKILL SW1's 'characterized exactly' should be replaced by: a sufficient condition for indexability.
Lineage step: the IPCO 1993 version became MOR 1996 with a student whose 1995 thesis it fed; companion papers with Paschalidis, Tsitsiklis and C.-P. Teo; PYI funding with a Draper match.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: unify classical algorithms as one algorithm on one polytope
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The c-mu rule, Smith's rule, Klimov's algorithm and the Gittins-index algorithms (including Varaiya-Walrand-Buyukkoc) all appear as adaptive greedy on an extended polymatroid, mapped in Tables 1-3.
The vertices of the achievable region are the n! static-priority orders, and one greedy pass finds the optimal one; compare S024's permutohull, handled by an assignment-LP dual.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: points of a convex region read as randomizations
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Any achievable performance vector is a randomization of at most n static-priority rules (Caratheodory); compare S033 (an SDP solution as a covariance) and S024 (a risk measure as a worst-case expectation over reweightings).

transferable: To prove a control problem is solved by a priority rule, find weights A_i^S and a set function b with a conservation law for each subset, tight when the outside classes have priority; Theorems 4-5 then give the region and the index policy (pp. 19-21).
Prove a greedy algorithm optimal by constructing its dual on a nested family, checking dual feasibility by induction and closing with complementary slackness (pp. 11-12).
Prove subset inequalities by a busy-period decomposition for the priority policy and a pairwise sample-path interchange for all other policies (pp. 23-24, 28-29).
Interpret an index as the break-even pension of an added retirement option; turn holding taxes into rewards by entrance charges and departure refunds (pp. 25, 30).
Run the method on the smallest nontrivial example before the general theory, and map prior results in a table of problem, criterion and who proved what (pp. 3, 5-8).

quotes.text: For the most part, the tradition for stochastic and dynamic scheduling problems has been, however, quite different, as it relies primarily on dynamic programming formulations.
Faced with these results, one asks what is the underlying reason that these nontrivial problems have very efficient solutions, both in theory and in practice.

title: Semidefinite relaxations, multivariate normal distributions, and order statistics
contribution: Rounds an SDP relaxation of boolean QP by sampling a normal vector with the SDP optimum as covariance, and proves: 0.878 for s-t max-cut; 0.878 for s-u-v max-cut, feasible with probability above 0.91; feasibility in expectation with violation bounds for linearly constrained boolean QP; a 0.878 cut with at least 32% of nodes per side. Adds an exact order-statistics bisection heuristic near 0.5, and a conjectured near-0.878 median-split heuristic tested on G-set graphs up to 3,000 nodes (read as the November 1997 preprint).
problem_entry: IO+CP: the Goemans-Williamson recipe (SDP relaxation plus geometric rounding) gave 0.878, 0.65 and 2/pi results (p. 4); no SDP guarantee existed for s-u-v max-cut (p. 4), and rounding must respect linear side constraints. Class: max x'Qx subject to linear equalities and x_j^2 = 1, with GB, ST-/ST+ and SUV instances (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Read the SDP optimum X* as a covariance, sample x ~ N(0, X*) and round by sign, so that Sheppard's 1900 formula E[x_i x_j] = (2/pi) arcsin(x*_ij) drives the analysis (pp. 5-7); split at the median of the sample for bisection (H2, H3, pp. 13-14). [My reading] H1 is distributed exactly like GW rounding (p. 6), so its novelty is the analysis; H3 is new.
assumptions: Symmetric Q, linear equality constraints (homogeneous, with Q PSD, in section 3.3) and boolean variables (pp. 3, 10); the SDP is assumed feasible, and its dual has an interior, so there is no gap (p. 5); data: Helmberg-Rendl G-set graphs from rudy, 800-3,000 nodes (p. 15).
proof_devices: Z_QP <= Z_SD via X = xx' (Proposition 1, p. 6)
Moments of the sign vector from Sheppard's orthant formula (Proposition 2, p. 7)
Almost-sure feasibility from a zero second moment (ST-), or from the zero variance of the square via the fourth moment (ST+) (Theorems 1-2, p. 8)
A sign-case lemma bounding a sum of arcsines, plus the trivariate orthant probability (Tong), for SUV feasibility above 0.912 (Lemma 1, Theorem 3, p. 9)

Matrix sandwich X + ((pi-2)/2) tr(X) I >= arcsin[X] >= X from the arcsin series and PSD Hadamard powers (Lemma 2, p. 10), giving feasibility in expectation, violation and 2/pi objective bounds (Theorem 4, pp. 10-11)
Second-moment bound 0.122 (e'a)^2 on the imbalance via the GW inequality, then Chebyshev and repetition, for a 32%-balanced 0.878 cut (Lemma 3, Theorem 5, pp. 12-13)
Exact order-statistics analysis of a median split via a beta integral (Theorem 6, pp. 13-14)
A heuristic argument in place of a proof for H3: the sample mean is exactly 0 since e'X*e = 0, so the median should be near 0 (p. 14)
experiments: G-set max-bisection: 54 graphs solved, 25 shown with no stated selection rule; columns are the SDP bound, H1's mean imbalance over 2,000 samples, H3's best of 2,000, and the ratio to the SDP bound, 0.7819-0.9819 (pp. 15-16); no times, machine, GW or Frieze-Jerrum baselines, or comment on the low-ratio families.
positioning: Credits GW for the central idea and cites Lovasz-Schrijver, Nesterov-Nemirovskii, Alizadeh, Frieze-Jerrum, Nesterov's 2/pi and Bellare-Rogaway (pp. 4-5, 12); claims only softly that GW's feasibility in expectation is 'not obvious' (p. 11), a property [my reading] GW shares by distributional equivalence; classical probability sources: Sheppard, Johnson-Kotz, Tong (pp. 5, 7, 9).
writing: Enumerated contributions mirrored in the abstract (pp. 2, 4-5); highlights the 1900 formula (p. 5); a conjecture stated among the contributions, backed by a labelled heuristic argument and a table (pp. 5, 14-16); no conclusion; two contribution-list results rounded up (the 0.5 is (1/2)(1-1/(n-1)), p. 14; the 0.878 for bisection needs only 32% balance, pp. 12-13).
limits_future: Stated: H3 unanalysed (p. 14); the constrained-QP result holds only in expectation (pp. 10-11). Unstated: no times or baselines, 29 of 54 graphs not shown, low ratios not discussed (p. 15). Future work is implicit in the conjecture (pp. 5, 14).

method_links.note: The boolean QP is relaxed to a polynomially solvable SDP, not kept in its class; the boundary is printed as approximation ratios, and the dual only rules out a gap. Reading the SDP solution as second moments echoes the moment line.
Each instance carries its certificate (the ratio to the SDP bound), but no incumbent rounding is run, no times are given, and H3 is scored by its best of 2,000 samples.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: relaxation solution read as a probability distribution and rounded by sampling
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The SDP optimum is a covariance matrix to sample from; compare S057's randomized priority rules and S024's reweighted samples.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: conjecture, labelled heuristic argument and computation when the proof fails
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: H3's analysis is called difficult; a heuristic argument and a 25-graph table support the near-0.878 conjecture.

transferable: Given an SDP relaxation with diag(X) = e, sample x ~ N(0, X) and round by sign; every pairwise statistic follows from E[x_i x_j] = (2/pi) arcsin(x_ij) (p. 7).
Show that a constraint survives rounding almost surely by computing the second (or fourth) moment of its residual from X and showing zero variance (p. 8).
Sandwich arcsin[X] between X and X + c tr(X) I, using the arcsin series and PSD Hadamard powers, to bound violation and objective at once (pp. 10-11).
For a balance constraint, bound the second moment of the imbalance, apply Chebyshev and resample until the cut is both good and balanced (pp. 12-13).
Analyse a median-split heuristic exactly, as an order-statistics event evaluated by a beta integral (pp. 13-14).
Report heuristic values as ratios to the relaxation bound, so that each instance carries its own certificate (p. 15).

quotes.text: The previous theorem shows that the solution produced by our method is feasible in expectation. It is not obvious that the Goemans-Williamson technique has this property.
Heuristically speaking, one would expect that the median and the sample mean would be close to each other

title: Constructing uncertainty sets for robust linear optimization
contribution: Shows that a coherent risk constraint on N samples is a robust linear constraint over an explicit convex set, and conversely; that distortion risk measures give polyhedral q-permutohulls, generated by N CVaR measures, whose LP counterparts need 2N extra variables and N^2 constraints; and that one LP gives the best centrally symmetric inner approximation of any polytope.
problem_entry: RO, with risk theory from finance: the RO literature is essentially silent on constructing uncertainty sets, and norm and ellipsoidal sets (Bertsimas et al. 2004 among them) are 'fundamentally ad hoc', chosen for tractability (p. 2). With only N samples and no construction rule (p. 4), the paper derives the set from the decision maker's coherent risk measure, for one uncertain linear constraint (pp. 2-5).
key_idea: The representation theorem (a coherent risk measure is a worst-case expectation over a family Q, p. 4) is a duality statement, so a risk constraint on samples equals a robust constraint over conv{Aq: q in Q} (Theorem 3.1, p. 5); distortion measures (coherent, comonotonic, law invariant, p. 7) give permutohulls generated by CVaR_{j/N} (Theorems 4.2-4.3, pp. 8-9).
assumptions: A single constraint, handled constraint-wise for several, since vector-valued risk is open (p. 4); a finite sample space of N data points, with admitted shortcomings (Assumption 3.1, p. 5); equal weights 1/N, with rational weights by replication at a size cost (Assumption 4.1, p. 7), critical for one direction of Lemma 4.1 (p. 8); no real data.
proof_devices: Representation theorem, plus: the inf of a linear function over a set equals its inf over the convex hull (Theorem 3.1, p. 5)
Examples: scenario sets; CVaR gives the convex hull of j-point averages; one-sided moments give norm-bounded sets (pp. 5-6)
Estimability argument: a measure that is not law invariant cannot be estimated consistently (p. 7)

Choquet representation (Schmeidler), law invariance and submodularity as nonincreasing second differences give concavity, then Follmer-Schied (Lemma 4.1, pp. 7-8); a counterexample shows equal weights are needed (p. 8)
Finite generation of the restricted simplex by N CVaR vectors with explicit weights (Theorem 4.2, p. 8)
Robust counterpart over a permutohull via strong duality of an assignment-type LP: 2N variables and N^2 constraints, O(N) for CVaR (Theorem 4.3, p. 9)
Central symmetry through the sample mean iff q = 2e_N - q_sigma; floor(N/2)+1 generators (Proposition 4.1, Theorem 4.4, pp. 9-11)
A Minkowski-functional norm and a scaling lemma give, by one LP, the largest inner approximation of a polytope (Proposition 4.2, Lemma 4.2, Theorem 4.5, pp. 11-13)
experiments: none: two-dimensional illustrations with N = 5 and N = 6 (Figures 1-4, pp. 9-13); tractability is argued by a size count (p. 9).
positioning: Within RO (Soyster, Ben-Tal-Nemirovski, El Ghaoui, Bertsimas et al. 2004, Bertsimas-Sim 2006, p. 2), a contribution to 'robust optimization, not risk theory' that borrows known risk results (p. 3); Natarajan et al. 2009 independently go from sets to risk measures (p. 3); chance constraints are set aside for nonconvexity (p. 5); his own 2004 sets are among those called ad hoc (p. 2).
writing: The abstract leads with the primitive (p. 2); numbered key results with the thesis sentence inside them, and a scope sentence (p. 3); plain admission of the samples' shortcomings (p. 5) and of Lemma 4.1's novelty status (p. 7); small examples for intuition (pp. 6-7).
limits_future: Limits: one constraint, LP only, samples only, no computation; the probability guarantee holds under the empirical distribution, and only roughly for atoms (pp. 4-5, 13). Future: multiple constraints and vector-valued risk; conic problems; information beyond samples, such as priors, moments and no-arbitrage (p. 13).

method_links.note: The class is kept: a set with up to N! vertices yields an LP with 2N variables and N^2 constraints, and the approximation is itself an LP; the boundary is printed (conic extension unclear, vector risk open). On step 3 the paper is a variant: it calls tractability-first set choice 'fundamentally ad hoc', derives the set first and proves tractability afterwards.

The knob is the decision maker's risk measure (the CVaR level j/N), and the set 'becomes a consequence' of it: a 2009 answer to arbitrary knobs. CVaR implies a chance bound under the empirical law. No price curve, no computation.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: derive the uncertainty set from a primitive the decision maker owns
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A coherent risk measure plus the samples determine the set through the representation theorem; the set 'becomes a consequence' of the risk measure chosen.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: permutation-indexed polytopes with small generator families
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Permutohulls have up to N! vertices but an LP counterpart; N CVaR generators span all distortion measures, and floor(N/2)+1 the symmetric subclass; compare S057's priority-order vertices.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: points of a convex region read as randomizations
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A coherent risk measure is a worst-case expectation over reweightings q of the samples, so the set is conv{Aq}; compare S057 p. 20 and S033 pp. 5-7.

transferable: Start an uncertainty set from a coherent risk measure and N samples, U = conv{Aq : q in Q}; for CVaR at level j/N with equal weights, U is the convex hull of all j-point averages of the data (pp. 5-6).

For a set that is the convex hull of all permuted weightings, write the robust constraint via the dual of the assignment LP over doubly stochastic weights: 2N variables and N^2 constraints, regardless of the vertex count (p. 9).
Prove finite generation by writing the class as a restricted simplex and exhibiting explicit nonnegative weights on its generators (p. 8).
Measure the conservatism of an arbitrary polytope by one LP that finds the largest scaled symmetric reference set around the sample mean that fits inside it (p. 12).
Justify an axiom by estimability: without law invariance, a risk measure cannot be estimated consistently from samples (p. 7).

quotes.text: This is important because the uncertainty set becomes a consequence of the particular risk measure the decision maker selects.
Moreover, this approach cannot capture events outside the set of samples.

title: Robust optimization for unconstrained simulation-based problems
contribution: Characterizes descent directions and robust local minima of the worst-case cost under implementation errors and proves convergence for convex costs given a worst-error oracle. The resulting gradient-based robust local search (n+1 ascents, SOCP moves away from high-cost neighbours) handles nonconvex simulation-based problems and is extended to parameter uncertainty. It is shown on a 2-D polynomial and a 100-dimensional electromagnetic design: worst case 8% lower at unchanged nominal cost.
problem_entry: RO+HS, with engineering design (AP) as testbed: distributions are 'seldom available' and chance constraints intractable (p. 1); robust methods cover only convex classes and 'cannot be applied' to costs defined by simulation (p. 2); joint implementation and parameter uncertainty are neglected (p. 2). Problem: minimize the worst case over an error ball for a nonconvex f given by its value and gradient (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: The descent directions of the worst-case cost are those with a negative inner product with all worst errors (Theorem 1, pp. 3-4), and an angle-maximizing SOCP finds one (p. 5); high-cost neighbours spanning the worst errors suffice (Proposition 2, pp. 5-6), which gives robust local search (pp. 6-8); parameters are folded in as pinned decision variables (p. 12).
assumptions: Unconstrained C^1 f with value and gradient from a subroutine (adjoint gradient in the EM case) (pp. 2, 11); an l2 error ball (p. 3); convergence needs convex f, bounded minima, an exact worst-error oracle and diminishing steps (p. 5); the practical method is 'a heuristic strategy', with conditions checked numerically (p. 6); Gamma = 550 um from a 40 um laboratory standard deviation at 99%, assuming independent normal errors (p. 12).
proof_devices: Danskin's min-max theorem for the directional derivative and convexity of the worst-case cost (Appendix A, p. 16)
KKT: the gradient at a worst error is parallel to it (Proposition 3, p. 16), which gives the descent characterization (Theorem 1, Appendix B, p. 17)
Typology of robust local minima; the type with an interior worst error can be a bad solution (Figure 2, p. 4)

Separating hyperplane: -d* lies in the convex hull of the worst errors (Proposition 4, p. 17), which is the subdifferential, so the method is a subgradient algorithm converging under Shor's step rules (Theorem 2, pp. 5, 17)
Cone-containment sufficient condition: moving away from a spanning set of bad neighbours is a descent (Proposition 2, pp. 5-6)

Algorithm design: a fixed barrier parameter for predictable inner-search time, n+1 structured ascents, reuse of a history set, a shrinking cost factor, a cosine-rule step and a direction recheck (pp. 6-8)
Parameter uncertainty by adding d_p = 0 to the direction SOCP (pp. 13-14)
experiments: 2-D polynomial: Gamma 0.5, a Gloptipoly-certified nominal minimum, two starts reaching one robust minimum, not generalizable (p. 8). 100-dim EM design with a laboratory-validated simulator (0.7 s per solve, p. 10): after 65 iterations the worst case is 8% lower and the nominal unchanged; random sampling with 30,000 evaluations reaches 96% of the algorithm's 3,000-evaluation estimate (p. 12). Parameter-uncertain polynomial: depth trade-off of n+1 ascents 600 s, 10+1 550 s, 3+1 non-terminating (pp. 14-15). No competing robust method is run.
positioning: Against stochastic programming (distributions seldom available, p. 1), multicriteria and tolerance methods of structural design (pp. 1-2), convex-only RO and minimax (p. 2; Appendix A, p. 16), polynomial SDP (too large, p. 8) and random-sampling perturbation analysis ('the standard today', p. 12); extends the authors' 2007 physics-journal method (p. 2); critique by scope only.
writing: Framed by analogy with gradient descent ('the same potential, but for the richer robust problem', p. 2); a 2-D figure for every concept (pp. 3-7); hedges in the body (pp. 8, 12); abstract and conclusion stronger than the body: 'significantly lower' is 8%, 'a number of different initial solutions' is two starts, and termination is called an 'optimality condition' (pp. 1, 8, 12, 15).
limits_future: Limits: convergence only for convex f with an exact oracle (p. 5); a heuristic method for nonconvex f (p. 6); an estimated worst case, open to late discoveries (p. 12); problem-dependent search depth (p. 15); unconstrained only. No future directions are stated (p. 15).

method_links.note: No reformulation keeps a solver class, because the cost is a simulation; the conic class survives only in the per-iteration direction SOCP; the polynomial-SDP alternative is rejected for its size; the boundary is printed as convex-only convergence.
Gamma is calibrated from measured error statistics, not fixed arbitrarily; the price is one point (worst case 8% lower, nominal unchanged), not a curve.

The nominally optimized design is both warm start and comparator, and random-sampling perturbation analysis is dueled at matched evaluation counts. But there is no certificate: the worst case is estimated and late discoveries are admitted, yet the conclusion calls termination an optimality condition.

The partner laboratory's data set Gamma and validate the simulator; the current practice (optimize, then test sensitivity by random simulation) is the baseline; the judgement is in simulation only, with no fabricated robust design.
Lineage and venue split: the application went to a physics journal in 2007, and the method followed in Operations Research.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: robust analogue of a classical algorithmic primitive
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Descent directions and local minima are redefined for the worst-case cost and characterized by theorem, and the algorithm is built by analogy with gradient descent and subgradient methods.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: fold one uncertainty type into another by lifting
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Parameter uncertainty becomes implementation error on extra variables pinned by equality constraints, so one algorithm treats both.

transferable: For a min-max over an error ball, characterize descent directions as those with a negative inner product with all worst errors, compute the best one by an angle-maximizing SOCP, and stop when it is infeasible (pp. 4-5).

Prove convergence by showing that -d* lies in the convex hull of the worst errors (separating hyperplane), that this hull is the subdifferential (Danskin plus KKT), and invoking the subgradient step rules (pp. 16-17).
When theory says the inner maximum need not be exact, fix the barrier parameter and use several short ascents from structured starts, buying predictable subproblem time (pp. 6-7).
Treat parameter uncertainty as implementation error on extra variables fixed by equality constraints, and add d_p = 0 to the direction problem (pp. 12-14).
Calibrate the size of the uncertainty set from measured error statistics and a coverage level, and validate the simulator against experiments before optimizing on it (pp. 10, 12).

Benchmark the worst-case estimator against random sampling at matched function-evaluation counts, and report the trade-off between inner-search depth and run time, including the setting that fails to terminate (pp. 12, 15).

quotes.text: Because we can only estimate the worst-case cost, there is always a chance for late discoveries of worst implementation errors.
The numerically determined termination criteria of the algorithm acts as an optimality condition for robust optimization problems.
